beats.trigger: ## Security
beats.got: nothing new, a module title

beats.trigger: You can't tell if your agent is safe from its output.
beats.got: Reading what an agent writes won't tell me whether it is safe, so I need a separate check.

beats.trigger: Prework covers personal skills and agent risk layered on normal security.
beats.got: There is homework I probably did not do, and it is about multi-agent things that don't sound like people questions.

beats.trigger: **Apply** named agent risk patterns (direct and indirect prompt injection, secrets in context, tool confusion, skill supply chain) and a plain access review
beats.got: A long list of terms I haven't heard explained yet. 'Skill supply chain' means nothing to me.

beats.trigger: Name what you'd want to check before letting this near a real stakeholder.
beats.got: I should think about what I'd want checked before this touches real people. That is a question I can work with.

beats.trigger: A tool call is text crossing a boundary into action.
beats.got: The agent turns its own text into actions through tools, so anything misleading in the text can become a misleading action.

beats.trigger: Would you bet your job on it being safe?
beats.got: Nobody can promise me certainty here, and that uneasy feeling is normal.

beats.trigger: same input, same output.
beats.got: Old software was predictable, so the old controls worked. Fine, I accept that.

beats.trigger: What may the agent read? What may it change? What must come back to a human?
beats.got: Three questions I can take to the leadership team, and I don't need to be technical to ask them.

beats.trigger: Scope (give the agent less). Split (two agents, different trust levels). Filter (post-process output). Gate (human approves). Review (a second agent judges).
beats.got: Five kinds of fix. I'll remember 'gate' because it means a human approves.

beats.trigger: **"I can't tell"** is a real answer.
beats.got: Writing down what remains and signing for it is a governance habit I already know from change negotiations.

beats.trigger: More context makes a good answer likelier. Less access makes a bad answer smaller.
beats.got: Giving an agent less access limits the damage, but it also makes the agent less useful.

beats.trigger: If that is where the biggest risk lives, a human drafts and the agent reviews.
beats.got: Sometimes the safest design keeps the human doing the sensitive work, for example anything touching employee data.

beats.trigger: Damn, this is complex stuff.
beats.got: It will stay complex, and what carries over is running the loop.

beats.trigger: A **skill** packages an expertise (rules, checklists, the moves an agent runs) into something the agent loads when the work matches.
beats.got: A skill is a reusable checklist the agent loads. That is close to something I could hand to an HR partner.

beats.trigger: they show which rules files can check and which need judgment, context, or a standing evidence check.
beats.got: Some rules can be checked by a machine and others need a person's judgment.

beats.trigger: the customer your CEO would not want named in a transcript.
beats.got: I describe in plain language what matters to us and the agent turns it into the check. I'd say employee data and works-council rules.

beats.trigger: Expect many questions; the agent keeps probing both lenses over several rounds.
beats.got: The agent will ask me a lot of questions, and I'm not sure I'll know the answers.

beats.trigger: Make the rules sound like your company's policy, not a generic GDPR template.
beats.got: I can hand questions back to the agent, but I have to make the rules sound like us.

beats.trigger: Run `ls .claude/skills/agent-audit/` to confirm.
beats.got: A technical save step. It's mechanics, and I'd have to ask someone which runtime I'm in.

beats.trigger: Agent mitigations sit on top of normal company controls, not in place of them.
beats.got: The agent checks don't replace legal and DPO controls.

beats.trigger: The goal is the loop (assess, mitigate, reassess residual), not a clean bill of health.
beats.got: I'm not looking for a pass. I'm practising the loop.

beats.trigger: Type `/` and look for `/agent-audit` in the autocomplete list.
beats.got: A third technical step in a row, and nobody has mentioned who owns this work.

beats.trigger: Expect the reusable check to find things you did not think about, and to leave things "I can't tell" you thought were settled.
beats.got: The check finds gaps in what I thought was settled, such as employee data going to a US tool.

beats.trigger: The uncomfortable feeling is the evidence.
beats.got: The discomfort is information. I should pay attention to it, not smooth it over.

beats.trigger: The risk remains. That is expected. Name it, accept it on record, and stop there.
beats.got: I fix one risk, write down what remains, and sign it off. That feels honest.

beats.trigger: The narrow question the expert can answer is sitting in the report. Walk in with that.
beats.got: I take a specific question to the DPO or works council with the evidence in hand. That is what I needed.

beats.trigger: Risk control, done for every risk you found, separates a prototype from a production agent.
beats.got: One risk fixed is a demo. A production agent needs all of them done, and that is a lot of work.

beats.trigger: The reusable check is the expert in the room, and it carries to the next agent.
beats.got: The check and the report are what I keep. I can reuse the check and show the report.

beats.trigger: The unease stays.
beats.got: The agent adds rules to the instructions file for future sessions, and the unease doesn't go away.

beats.trigger: To share, give a teammate the skill and install it in their runtime.
beats.got: I could package a method, like reviewing how we use employee data, and give it to HR partners. That is how a habit spreads.

beats.trigger: Mitigations add to security controls, never replace them.
beats.got: Four lines that sum up the module.

beats.trigger: Your call.
beats.got: Homework, with a mild guilt trip attached.

beats.trigger: What check was missing around the agent's output?
beats.got: Two real failure cases to read, which sounds useful for my leadership team.

take_homes: Nobody gets certainty with agents. Run a loop: check, make one fix, write down what remains, decide and sign.
Giving an agent less access is the cheapest fix. For employee data, a human might do the sensitive part.
When 'I can't tell' shows up, take the report and one narrow question to the DPO, legal or the works council.

monday.move: Ask my HR business partners and the DPO what data a people-metrics agent would touch, and whether we need the works council before trying one
monday.who: One HR business partner and our DPO
monday.when: Monday morning, 30 minutes before the leadership meeting prep
monday.stop_condition: If the DPO says employee data can't go into the tool, I stop and don't build anything
monday.blocker: I haven't yet asked the works council or the DPO, and I don't know the answer on employee data.

misconception.why: The module never discussed roles or headcount. It was about safety and risk, so my belief that agents replace headcount first and the question is which roles go was neither tested nor changed.

one_line: Useful for learning that you can't get certainty and should keep a record of what's left, but it was all about the tool and nobody talked about people.
